articles.title: Fed avvaktar men höjer senare i år
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
USA-börserna stängde på plus igår; S&P500 steg med 0,6% och mer tekniktunga Nasdaq med 1,2%. Under natten är utvecklingen i Asien blandad men mest upp på förnyad tech-optimism. Japanska Nikkei har stigit med drygt 1% men bäst går det i Sydkorea (upp över 6%) där teknikaktier driver utvecklingen efter att bl a SK Hynix levererat en stark rapport och utlovat höga utdelningar. I väntan på Fed-besked och viktiga bolagsrapporter, idag från bl a Microsoft och Alphabet, pekar terminer svagt ner i Europa och svagt upp i USA inför dagens handel. Brasiliens Bolsonaro har landat i USA efter att ha förlorat valet i Brasilien. Oljepriser har stigit något över natten efter rapportering om att USA sagt åt länderna kring Persiska viken att förbereda sig på ett kort men intensivt anfall efter USA:s mellanårsval. 
Centralbanksfokus i dagens kalender.
 Dagens statistik har stort centralbanksfokus med besked från Fed och Kanada (mer nedan). Tyskt konsumentförtroende (GfK) kan ge lite ledtrådar kring tyska ekonomin och hur det går med tillväxtåterhämtningen. 
Splittrat val i Israel. 
Stödet ser ut att bli ungefär lika stort för Netanyahus regerande koalition och oppositionens block samtidigt som antalet parlamentsledamöter för arabiska partier (utanför båda blocken) ökar; en svår regeringsbildning även för Israel. 
Fed: Annat än en oförändrad ränta skulle vara en stor överraskning – räntehöjning kommer i december.
 Efter mjukare kommentarer från vissa Fed-ledamöter och lite mer nervösa börser den senaste tiden prissätter marknaden en sannolikhet på över 90 procent för ett oförändrat räntebesked. Utsikterna är osäkra och viktigt är den pågående konflikten i Mellanöstern, styrkan i den amerikanska ekonomin och utvecklingen av de finansiella förhållandena. Vi håller fast vid vår bedömning att Fed höjer räntan ytterligare en gång i december, följt av räntesänkningar mot slutet av 2027 och under första halvåret 2028. Läs Elisabet Kopelmans Fed Preview 
här
. 
Oförändrat från Nya Zeeland, Kanada väntas höja.
 Under natten lämnade Nya Zeelands centralbank, i ett splittrat besked, oväntat räntan oförändrad med hänvisning till att global osäkerhet tynger ekonomin; valutan föll på beskedet. Kanadas centralbank väntas höja från 2,25 till 2,50% när inflationen stiger och BNP ökar i god takt. 
Brittisk budget skjuter på de svåra besluten.
 Premiärminister Burnham har ambitiösa planer för att få igång ekonomin men politiken är bakbunden av redan höga skatter och stora underskott. Budgetförslaget som presenteras idag är med tanke på höga räntor och offentligfinansiellt fokus intressant för både politiskt intresserade och marknader. Troligen blir det en försiktig budget med fokus på hushåll och småföretag med förhoppning om att inte göra marknaden nervös och att utrymmet för att finansiera ytterligare reformer kommer att öka om tillväxt tar fart och energipriser och räntor faller. Läs mer 
här
. 
Lästips: Dagens Ögat är fullmatad med spännande läsning.
 Vi går igenom förutsättningarna inför mellanårsvalet i USA den 3 november. Huvudscenariot är en demokratisk seger i båda kongressens kamrar, men utgången i senaten är fortfarande osäker. Vi gör även ett centralbankssvep samt analyserar de stigande varupriserna i euroområdet. Avslutningsvis resonerar vi kring det potentiella skiftet på valutamarknaden. Du hittar ögat 
här
.

 Med dagens analys av 
Japan

Researchsida
. Den 10 november publicerar vi vår sammantagna globala syn inklusive alla sedvanliga och efterlängtade prognostabeller.

articles.title: Vad ändras med en demokratisk storseger?
articles.heading: Ögat
articles.fulltext:
Mellanårsvalet i USA står för dörren. En demokratisk seger i båda kongressens kamrar är huvudscenariot, men utgången i senaten är fortfarande osäker. En seger i representanthuset räcker för att blockera republikanernas finanspolitiska agenda, men president Trump behåller i båda fallen makten över utrikes-, immigrations- och handelspolitiken. 
Riksbanken höjer trots lägre inflation
Det mesta talar för att Riksbanken höjer styrräntan till 2 procent den 4 november. Direktionen har varit tydlig i sin kommunikation och trots att inflationen har blivit lägre än väntat tror vi på en höjning. Vi räknar också med att Riksbanken håller fast vid sin tidigare prognos med ytterligare höjningar nästa år. 
Globala centralbanksbeskeden duggar tätt
Vi befinner oss i en intensiv centralbanksperiod där i stort sett alla de centralbanker vi följer kommer att ge besked om räntan. Vi räknar med en höjning från Riksbanken, Bank of England, Bank of Canada och Reserve Bank of Australia, medan övriga förväntas lämna sina styrräntor oförändrade. 
Stigande varupriser i euroområdet beror inte på krigen
Varupriserna i euroområdet har stigit gradvis i år och inflationstakten ligger tydligt över det historiska genomsnittet. Men medan ECB:s fokus legat på indirekta effekter av högre energipriser, verkar uppgången hittills bero på ett skifte i ökningstakten för elektronikvaror. 
JPY och SEK kan gynnas av potentiellt marknadsskifte
Valutamarknadens fokus på högräntevalutor, vilket bland annat gett stöd åt dollarn, ser alltmer ut att gå mot ett skifte. Positioneringen är ansträngd och lägre energipriser och fallande räntor skulle ge stöd till lågräntevalutor som japanska yenen och den svenska kronan.

articles.title: Nordic Outlook Update - Japan
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Eng)
articles.fulltext:
Our publication of Nordic Outlook in November has a slightly different format compared to other editions during the year. Under the heading Nordic Outlook Update , we are continuously publishing our forecasts and our macro view for individual countries/regions. On Tuesday 10 November, we will publish our overall view on growth, inflation, interest rates, etc., together with the table of all forecasts.
Policymakers are walking a tightrope as bond yields trade at multi-decade highs and the yen remains undervalued. The government must ease market concerns about public debt dynamics. Meanwhile, the Bank of Japan intends to normalise monetary policy as underlying inflation is close to the 2 per cent target. Japan’s economy has proven resilient, with domestic demand supported by high wage growth, fiscal stimulus, AI-demand supporting exports and a solid investment cycle. Growth is constrained by global risks and uncertainty over energy supply.
Japan’s government debt in relation to GDP, which is exceptionally high by international standards, will continue to decline in the coming years as nominal growth strengthens. Moreover, the debt is financed by domestic savings and central bank holdings, making it less dependent on foreign financing. However, debt dynamics are a bit worrisome. The duration of the public debt is around 9 years. When borrowing costs rise, and remain above long-term potential growth, domestic investors may demand compensation for increasing credit risks. 
The Takaichi government’s focus on expansionary economic policy (including a supportive monetary policy) – and signs that Japan has permanently left deflation behind – is testing markets. Risks to growth remain skewed to the downside over the forecast horizon. 
Domestic investment to support growth has long been insufficient. To raise potential growth, Japan is promoting investment in strategic sectors through close cooperation between the public and private sectors. High corporate profits, together with expectations of stronger productivity growth, should continue to support the domestic investment cycle.
To reduce the burden on low- and middle-income workers, the government will introduce benefits tailored to income levels on a full scale from FY2029. Japan will implement a two-year VAT reduction on food and beverages (from 8 to 2 per cent, starting in April 2027). Tokyo says that these measures will be financed without relying on deficit-financing bonds. Japanese policymakers are walking a tightrope as bond yields trade at multi-decade highs.
Nominal and real interest rates are expected to remain well below those in, for example, the US. Although rates remain low, they are higher than before, creating some headwinds for economic growth. The real policy rate will remain negative throughout the forecast period. 
Still, the yen is expected to receive support from (1) narrowing policy rate differentials with the US and the euro area, and (2) domestic financial investors who now find Japanese bond yields more attractive (hence limiting Japan’s export of capital to other countries). Over the forecast horizon, the current account surplus is expected to amount to USD 585bn.

articles.title: NOK 2bn in NST481 and NST490
articles.heading: NGB Spotlight
articles.fulltext:
On Wednesday Oct 28th, Norges Bank will hold a multiple tap auction where a total of NOK 2bn will be issued, split between the NST481 (1.75%, 09/2029) and the NST490 (4.125%, 06/2036) bonds. NST481 currently trades with a yield of 4.77%, implying a maturity-matched spread vs. Germany of 173bps and an ASW spread of -31.5bps. NST490 trades with a yield of 4.46%, with corresponding spread levels at 110bps and -12.25bps. The auction closes at 11.00 CET, and results will be available on Norges Bank’s website at 11.05 CET. 
Details
On Wednesday, Norges Bank will auction a total of NOK 2bn split between NST481 (09/2029) and the NST490 (06/2036) bonds. The longer tenor has been included in 11 auctions so far this year, as Norges Bank is aiming to build liquidity in the new 10y bond. The bond was also included in last week’s tap auction, where performance continued to be strong. So far this year, the bond has received an average bid-to-cover of 3.41 with an allotment share of 59%. The corresponding numbers for the 5 auctions in NST481 are 3.74 and 47%. We are not surprised that Norges Bank chooses to issue these bonds in the upcoming auction, and with the total volume capped at NOK 2bn we expect the auction to run smoothly.
Global bond markets have experienced significant volatility over the past month, with yields spiking sharply in early October before partially retracing. The 10Y US Treasury yield peaked at approximately 5.31% on Oct 5th before retracing and currently trading at ~5.00 %, while the 10Y Bund peaked near 3.49% and has since pulled back to 3.35%. NSTs have followed the global move: the 10Y NST yield reached a high of ~4.70% in early October and has since corrected to 4.46%, helping to stabilize spreads vs. Germany. NST ASW spreads continue to move largely sideways with lurking sellers in the mid-segment of the curve. Meanwhile, outright levels continue to attract demand from internationals. 
Expectations for Norges Bank have eased somewhat compared to last week with the market now discounting a 50/50 chance for another rate hike in December 2026 and still pricing in a full hike by March 2027. We reiterate our forecast that the hiking cycle has likely peaked, with policy easing not expected to begin before late 2027. Our inflation forecast is higher than Norges Bank’s near-term trajectory, but we predict slightly lower core inflation in 2027. 
Supply update: Following this auction, Norges Bank has issued a total of NOK 101bn YTD, while the annual borrowing interval is set at NOK 100-110bn (107-110bn in the Q4 guidance). We expect Norges Bank to issue the maximum amount, implying NOK 3bn in one of the 4 remaining auctions and NOK 2bn for the remaining auctions.
Supply 2027:
 The government’s budget proposal for 2027 showed an underlying borrowing requirement of NOK 93.6bn vs. 95.7bn in 2026. After years of under-borrowing, Norges Bank’s supply estimate has exceeded the underlying borrowing requirement over the past two years, with the aim of building up the cash reserves. We expect this to be the case also in 2027, implying a minimum of NOK 110bn in gross supply. The government’s borrowing mandate in long-term debt is increased by NOK 50bn to NOK 200bn, to provide greater flexibility and allowing for a potential increase in its own holdings. Risks to our supply estimate are thus skewed to the upside. Details will be provided in Norges Bank’s Strategy and borrowing programme due in December.

articles.title: Physicla risk meets capital
articles.heading: Sustainable Finance Outlook
articles.fulltext:
The latest issue of SEB’s Sustainable Finance Outlook highlights a stark reality: the energy transition is too slow to avert material physical climate risks. It examines exposure to these risks at fund, company and asset levels, and how sustainable finance can strengthen climate resilience. The report also explores water as both a systemic financial risk and an investment opportunity. 
Climate risk exposure scores across investment funds
Source: SEB, S&P 
Energy transition update
While the transition is still underway and electrification is gaining pace, it is too slow to prevent global warming from causing economic damage. Substantial investment is now needed both for mitigation and adaptation. Investors and companies need to know where physical risks are likely to emerge and how to limit the economic and financial damage.
Sustainable finance market update
Sustainable bonds reached USD 1598bn resulting in a 15% YOY growth despite geopolitical turmoil. Corporate issuers generally allocate only a small share of sustainable finance to investments in climate resilience. By contrast, the most climate-hazard-exposed holdings in selected investment funds have allocated a substantially higher share to climate resilience than MSCI ACWI companies overall. Asset-level assessment is essential to assess whether sustainable finance can reduce companies’ vulnerability to physical risks and protect investors from financial impacts.
Regulatory update
Regulators, standard setters and financial institutions increasingly expect physical climate risk to be translated into financial consequences and credible adaptation responses. Across corporate reporting, sustainable finance and prudential supervision, frameworks are converging on a more location-specific and forward-looking assessment process, even as differences in materiality, methodology and data continue to constrain comparability.
Asset level physical risk analysis
Asset-level insights from SEB’s Physical Risk Intelligence Tool reveal location-specific and overlapping climate exposures in mining holdings and data centres. Two case studies highlight material physical risk exposure at a mining company’s Chilean properties and identify 48 European data centres with significant exposure to a hazard combination that could strain electricity systems without effective adaptation measures.
Water: from systemic risk to bankable opportunity  
Water is fundamental to economic growth, industrial production and societal development. Yet ageing infrastructure, persistent underinvestment, pollution and growing demand are putting water systems under increasing pressure, while climate change brings increasing unpredictability through droughts and floods. This article sets out why water is becoming a material financial risk and how SEB is working with clients to turn it into bankable opportunities.

articles.title: Oil on edge with fear of new attacks on Iran after US midterm elections
articles.heading: Crude oil comment
articles.fulltext:
A slight pause after a rally to a high of $117.45/b last Friday. But market is on edge. 
The Brent Dec-26 contract has paused a little over the past two days with a price this morning of around $116.5/b. That is a strong upwards gain since the M1 Brent contract traded at around $102/b in early October with intraday low all the way down to $96.55/b on 1 October.
Trump's threats of massive new attacks on Iran sent crude sharply higher in October.
 Trump started in mid-September to talk about "approaching a major decision" to resume massive attacks on Iran or not. Reach a deal or destroy Iran was Trump's line in late September. Through October this line of argument has been reiterated. In addition there has been increasing reports that the US military was developing new strike plans, starting to move more military material towards the Persian Gulf and preparing for new, extensive combat activities.
To strike or not, that is the question.
 The impression now is that there is a significant risk premium in crude oil prices for the risk that the US/Israel will attack Iran in the coming weeks. Donald Trump has clearly wanted to delay fresh strikes against Iran till after the US midterm elections on 3 November, while Netanyahu wanted fresh strikes before today's Israeli elections. Netanyahu risks losing power as he is criticized for not having bombed Iran enough. The US republicans and Trump risks losing congressional power (the House and possibly the Senate) due to high gasoline and diesel prices with too much bombing of Iran.
The price to strike could be high. Risk of more lasting energy infrastructure damage.
 The price to strike hard at Iran now might be high. The US/Israel has already done it again and again and achieved very little. The US/Israeli argument is to bomb Iran until it concedes to all the demands of the US/Israel. Not the least to hand over 440 kg of highly enriched uranium. Very little chance of that happening. If the US/Israel strikes at Iranian energy infrastructure, then Iran will respond in kind. Risk then is much more lasting energy supply disruption from the Middle East until infrastructure has been repaired and that could take quite a bit of time.
Hectic efforts to defuse the situation and avoid fresh strikes. 
Iran yesterday hosted a meeting in Tehran where security, defense and intelligence ministers from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met to discuss the situation. Obviously all wanting to prevent fresh attacks from US/Israel. At another meeting, Oman's foreign minister Badr Albusaidi said that: the Gulf can “no longer rely upon the co-operation of external partners” (i.e. the US). And further that the Gulf states’ goal should be to reach a non-aggression pact with Iran, saying any regional “security architecture that doesn’t include them is inherently unstable” 
(FT today)
. This shows the direction of developments in the Middle East. The US is no longer going to be the key security provider in the region. The countries there have to be in charge of security and stability. And Iran will have to be an integrated part of the security solution. 
Oil at sea continues to rise. 
Oil at sea reached 1357 mb on 25 October which is getting close to the 7 Dec 2025 high of 1381 mb when Brent traded at $62/b. Not quite comparable since ships are sailing much longer journeys today. But oil at sea rising strongly and by 145 mb since late August with continued rise, indicates that oil is flowing out of the Middle East. From Yanbu into the Red Sea, through the SoH and also out through the UAE ADCOP pipeline. Varying measures of how much is exported from week to week. But overall the exports looks to be in the range of 15-18 mb/d in October overall. Though what the flow has been over the past week is uncertain.

articles.title: Anthropic revived stock markets, but shock in Brazil
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
Stock markets started the week in a better mood 
in both Europe and the US, while oil prices have fallen slightly from recent highs. In the US, the stock market was boosted by the news that Anthropic, which among other things is behind the AI model Claude, has submitted an application for listing on Nasdaq. At the same time, Meta announced that it is planning a new share issue of USD 95 billion to finance its AI investments. Asian stock markets are mixed, with rising equity prices in Japan and IT-heavy Korea, but down in Shanghai. Stock market futures are pointing slightly up in the US but down in Europe. In Brazil, markets reacted with shock to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's unexpected election win over Flávio Bolsonaro, triggering a fall of close to 8% for the currency and 14% on the stock market. The market's concern is that Lula will continue on the path of rising budget deficits and interest rates. Bolsonaro's party has now recognized Lula as the winner. 
Otherwise, markets are awaiting 
this and next week's interest rate announcements from almost all the major central banks and the US midterm elections. Market pricing for the Fed has crept higher with the support of slightly calmer markets, but still points to a very high probability of unchanged policy rates tomorrow. Betting odds and opinion polls still point to a Democratic victory in the entire Congress, but the margins are small in several important Senate elections. A Democratic sweep would block Trump's fiscal agenda and new appointments to among others the Fed, but not impede the White House much in other areas such as foreign, immigration and trade policy. At the same time, the Democrats' ability to push through their own policies will be limited by Trump's veto, and any initiatives from the Democrats will probably be more about testing the policies ahead of the 2028 presidential election. From the US and Canada we are getting signals of progress in the trade talks. President Trump decided the other day to ease some of the import tariffs to support Maine's Republican Senator Susan Collins ahead of the midterm elections. 
Household well-being is the focus of today's agenda
, with consumer confidence surveys in both France and the US, and in the US also durable goods orders and housing data. The question is how French consumers have been affected by the recent sharp rise in bond yields and the violent mass demonstrations. In the US, consumer sentiment remained near the lows in October, according to the Michigan index. The Conference Board's index has held up better but has also fallen recently. We are particularly interested to see households' views on the labour market, where the difference between those who believe "jobs are plentiful" and those who believe "jobs are hard to get" tends to correlate with unemployment. 
Deadlock ahead of Israel
's
 general elections today.
 According to most opinion polls before the election, the opposition, led by former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, looks set to win over prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu but without reaching the necessary majority of 61 in the Knesset. Arab parties, which several opposition parties have declined to govern with, 
will likely hold the swing vote
. If no government can be formed, Israel may go to the polls again early next year and Netanyahu will get to lead an interim government until then. According to Israeli newspapers, the current IDF chief of staff has opposed a request from Netanyahu to attack Iran shortly before the election, something that could have led to the election being canceled. According to CNN, Netanyahu has also tried to get Trump to agree to a joint attack.

A November hike from the Riksbank
 looks close to certain, but we still think that the market is pricing in too many hikes further ahead. Read more in our Sweden 360 
here
. The PPI for consumer goods rose less than expected yesterday. Today we get foreign trade and household lending.

articles.title: Anthropic livade upp börserna, men chock i Brasilien
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Börserna har hämtat nytt mod i början av veckan 
i både Europa och USA, samtidigt som oljepriset backat något från de senaste topparna. I USA fick börsen skjuts av beskedet om att Anthropic, som ligger bakom bl a AI-modellen Claude, lämnat in en ansökan om notering på Nasdaq. Samtidigt meddelade Meta att man planerar en nyemission på 95 miljarder USD för att finansiera sina AI-investeringar. Asiatiska börser är blandade, med stigande kurser i Japan och IT-tunga Korea, men ner i Shanghai. Börsterminerna pekar svagt upp i USA men ner i Europa. I Brasilien reagerade marknaderna med chock på Luiz Inácio Lula da Silvas oväntade valvinst över Flávio Bolsonaro, vilket utlöste ett fall på nära 8% för valutan och 14% på börsen. Marknadens oro är att Lula ska fortsätta på den inslagna vägen med stigande budgetunderskott och räntor. Bolsonaros parti har nu erkänt Lula som vinnare. 
I övrigt råder avvaktan 
inför denna och nästa veckas räntebesked från nästan alla de stora centralbankerna och USA:s mellanårsval. Marknadens inprisning av Fed har krupit upp med stöd av lite lugnare marknader, men pekar fortfarande mot en mycket hög sannolikhet för oförändrad ränta i morgon. Bettingodds och opinionsmätningar pekar alltjämt mot demokratisk seger i hela kongressen, men marginalerna är små i flera viktiga senatsval. Storslam för demokraterna skulle blockera Trumps finanspolitiska agenda och nya utnämningar till bl a Fed, men inte sätta stopp för Vita huset inom andra områden som utrikes-, immigrations- och handelspolitiken. Demokraternas möjlighet att själva driva igenom sin politik kommer samtidigt begränsas av Trumps veto och eventuella initiativ från demokraterna kommer nog snarare handla om att testa politiken inför presidentvalet 2028. Från USA och Kanada kommer signaler om framsteg i handelssamtalen. President Trump beslutade häromdagen att lätta på en del av importtullarna för att stötta Maines republikanska senator Susan Collins inför valet. 
Hushållens mående står i fokus för dagens agenda
, med konsumentförtroendemätningar i både Frankrike och USA, samt i USA även orderingång och husdata. Frågan är hur franska konsumenter har påverkats av den senaste tidens kraftiga uppgångar i obligationsräntorna och de våldsamma massdemonstrationerna. I USA låg konsumenthumöret enligt Michiganindexet kvar nära bottennivåer i oktober. Conference Boards index har hållit emot bättre men har också fallit på senare tid. Vi håller särskilt ögonen på hushållens syn på arbetsmarknaden där differensen mellan de som anser att det är ”gott om jobb” och de som anser att det är ”svårt att hitta ett jobb” tenderar att korrelera med arbetslösheten. 
Låst läge när Israel går till val idag.
 Enligt de flesta opinionsmätningarna inför valet ser oppositionen, ledd av förre ÖB Gadi Eisenkot, ut att vinna över premiärminister Benjamin Netanyahu men utan att nå den nödvändiga majoriteten på 61 i Knesset. Arabiska partier ser ut att bli vågmästare vilka flera oppositionspartier sagt nej till att regera med. Om ingen regering kan bildas kan Israel komma att gå till val på nytt i början av nästa år och Netanyahu får till dess leda en tillfällig regering. Enligt israeliska tidningar har nuvarande ÖB motsatt sig en begäran från Netanyahu att attackera Iran strax före valet, något som hade kunnat leda till att valet ställdes in. Enligt CNN har Netanyahu även försökt få Trump att gå med på en gemensam attack.

articles.title: Playing curveballs
articles.heading: Sweden 360
articles.fulltext:
Sweden 360 provides you with a quick and broad overview of Swedish macro, rates and FX.
*** See attachment for full report ***
Macro highlights: Riksbank Preview
November hike close to certain. 
We expect the Riksbank to raise the policy rate by 25bps to 2.00% on 4 November, supported by hawkish signals from Governor Thedéen. Minutes showed that a majority of Board members are likely to support a November hike. With no new forecasts or rate path, focus will be on forward guidance.
Lower core inflation unlikely to delay tightening. 
Core inflation has undershot the Riksbank’s forecast, but stronger growth and renewed upward pressure from energy prices support a November hike. 
Labour
 market signals have been mixed.
Rate guidance likely unchanged. 
We expect the Riksbank to reaffirm its September rate path, 
signalling
 another hike in Q1 2027, while highlighting continued upside inflation risks from persistently high energy prices.
Market focus on timing and risks. 
With a November hike largely anticipated, the key market driver will be signals about subsequent tightening. We forecast further hikes in February and May, followed by a rate cut in 2028. A stronger krona and less hawkish ECB could reduce pressure for further tightening. 
Riksbank Preview 
here
.
Rates highlights - Front-end views
Maintaining a view that the relative catch-up of Riksbank vs ECB is overpriced 
in 1Y1Y space. Look to range trade 1Y1Y Stibor vs ESTR but need caution as French turmoil could be seen as hampering ECB’s ability to hike. 
However, should 
ECB signal that QT could be stopped 
and that the QE portfolio reinvestments could be tilted to the French short-end for ’monetary policy trans-mission’ arguments it would likely solidify the view of additional ECB hikes.
Bias to receive March 2027 FRA on pricing 70bps (or more) hikes in the coming four meetings. 
However, can be a ’risky’ outright receive should we see esca-
lation
 in the 
Middle
East 
after US midterms. Possibly paying March BOE meeting against could be a hedge.
Rates highlights - Belly should be the allocation sweet spot
Global forces are pushing for higher ‘term-premia’ / steeper curves. 
Should central banks have to get more aggressive on 
e.g.
escalation in the Middle-East then would expect curves to invert into the belly. 
Should we 
move towards a diplomatic solution in the Middle-East there is too much premium for hikes in front-end which would benefit belly more than long-end 
where structural steepening forces are at play. 
From a Fixed Income allocation perspective this would argue that 2YF1Y to 3YF2Y is an optimal allocation point.
FX highlights - We remain bearish on NOKSEK in the medium-term – near-term dependent on escalation/diplomacy
Upcoming Data and Events
We see slight upside risks to the Riksbank’s Q3 GDP forecast (0.4%, 2.9% vs 0.2%, 2.7%. 
Flash GDP (Thu) is not reliable but private sector production and household consumption support stronger growth. Risk for a setback in especially consumer confidence (Thu) on the back of sharply higher energy prices. 
Retal sales (Thu) are expected to continue to rise, but risk for a downward revision to August.
PPI (Mon) increased sharply in September 3.4%, 11.2% y/y, but PPI on consumer goods are still muted (0.4%, 0.6% y/y) and significantly lower than expected in September.
The momentum for Swedish growth is currently very strong, but headwinds from high energy 
prices 
and rate hikes over the next 3-6 months are clear downside risks.

articles.title: Upcoming Budget - Kicking the can down the road
articles.heading: United Kingdom
articles.fulltext:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has ambitious plans to reshape the UK economy, and markets have been bracing for a potentially significant Budget on 28 October. However, with gilt yields elevated and markets on alert, alongside signs of an economic recovery, we expect a relatively modest Budget, primarily focused on supporting households and laying the groundwork for future reforms. The more difficult spending decisions will likely be postponed until 2027. With markets already pricing in a cautious Budget, the scope for a positive surprise appears limited, while an unexpectedly expansionary package could push gilt yields higher and sterling lower.
Cautious start but ambitious long-term agenda. 
The Burnham government has so far introduced relatively modest measures aimed at supporting households and addressing everyday concerns. Whether this reflects a genuine focus on voters’ needs or simply limited fiscal headroom is for the reader to decide. Nevertheless, the strategy appears to have helped Labour recover in the polls, regaining its position as the largest party ahead of Reform UK.
However, the government’s longer-term ambitions are considerably greater. The Manchesterism strategy emphasizes greater public control over essential infrastructure and services, increased housing construction, stronger regional economies, a greater focus on vocational training and youth unemployment, as well as higher defence spending and closer cooperation with the EU. The spending ambitions far exceed what even generous fiscal assumptions could accommodate. 
Political constraints make the fiscal arithmetic harder.
 Burnham and Healey have pledged to retain the previous government's fiscal rules, requiring the current budget to be in surplus and public sector net financial liabilities (PSNFL) to fall as a share of GDP by 2029/30. The government has also promised not to raise the main taxes on working households, including income tax, VAT and National Insurance, which together account for 54% of total tax revenues. These commitments significantly constrain Healey's room for long-term reforms. 
Resilient growth, but inflation risks are rising.
 The UK economy has remained surprisingly resilient, reducing the immediate need for fiscal stimulus. GDP grew by 0.6% quarter-on-quarter in Q1 and 0.5% in Q2, while growth remained solid over the summer. Business investment has increased, partly supported by higher spending on infrastructure and technology. Household consumption has also benefited from improving real incomes, and with the saving ratio still elevated at 8.8%, there is scope for a further recovery.
However, renewed inflationary pressures complicate the outlook. Headline inflation accelerated to 3.5% in September, while core inflation rose to 2.8% and services inflation to 3.7%. Higher energy prices, driven by the Middle East conflict, are eroding households' purchasing power, while rising producer prices suggest inflationary pressures in the pipeline. With inflation moving further above the BoE's target, we expect additional monetary tightening. Meanwhile, falling vacancies and weak payroll employment signal a soft labour market and with consumer confidence plunging in October, the risk of a faltering recovery is substantial.
Elevated yields reduce fiscal headroom. 
The 10-year gilt yield reached around 5.5% in early October, its highest level since 2007, while the 30-year yield briefly exceeded 6%. Although yields have since declined somewhat, borrowing costs remain elevated. With public sector net debt at 94% of GDP, substantial refinancing needs ahead and a relatively large share of inflation-linked debt, the UK particularly exposed. The recent global bond sell-off shows that investors are increasingly scrutinizing countries with weak public finances and are quick to demand higher risk premia. So far, France has been at the centre of attention, but market attention could quickly shift to the UK if the Budget raises concerns about fiscal credibility.
In March, the OBR projected fiscal headroom of £23.6bn against the current-budget rule and £27.1bn against the PSNFL investment rule. More recent estimates suggest that headroom against the current-budget rule could narrow to around £10–15bn, leaving the government with a relatively small buffer against further shocks.
What does this mean for the Budget? 
 The government's political ambitions and constraints, alongside the economic and financial backdrop, point towards a cautious Budget. Healey needs to demonstrate that the government is delivering on its promises and supporting the economic recovery while preserving market confidence and ensuring compliance with the fiscal rules.
Household and small business support is therefore likely to be the main spending priority, potentially amounting to £4bn. With higher energy prices having eroded the benefits of earlier measures, further assistance with energy bills is likely. Relief for small businesses is also expected, potentially through an increase in the business rates relief threshold. Temporary support measures that expire before 2029/30 would have limited direct impact on fiscal headroom in the target year, although they would still increase near-term borrowing.
For the more structural themes, the Budget will need to address the remaining £4.7bn funding gap over four years in the Defence Investment Plan. It will also provide further details on previously announced regional devolution and investment reforms, including changes allowing related local projects to be assessed together and a lower social discount rate, which increases the present value of long-term investment benefits. More ambitious reforms, including regional income tax sharing, social care and the longer-term increase in defence spending, will largely be left for the 2027 Spending Review.
With constraints on the revenue side, Healey will need to rely on smaller tax changes to finance spending. An increase in the bank corporation tax surcharge has emerged as a leading possibility, potentially raising around £2bn annually. Changes to property taxes and selected tax reliefs could also be considered. However, reports suggest the Chancellor has ruled out higher capital gains tax rates, reflecting concerns about private investment and the economic recovery.
Risks and potential market reactions. 
Our base case is a relatively cautious Budget that preserves around £10–15bn of fiscal headroom, and maintains a credible fiscal trajectory. This should have limited implications for gilt yields or sterling, as well as for the economy. A larger buffer could provide some support for gilts by reducing fiscal uncertainty.
A potential risk is excessive use of public financial institutions (PuFins) to expand investment without breaching the fiscal rules. Under the PSNFL framework, borrowing to finance loans or equity investments can be offset by the financial assets acquired, leaving the headline debt measure largely unchanged. However, that still requires additional gilt issuance and entails financial risks, particularly if the assets fail to deliver the expected returns.
Another concern is reliance on optimistic assumptions about future growth or tax revenues to justify spending commitments. Comparing earlier prime ministers' pre-Budget speeches with Burnham's communication suggests that he places considerable emphasis on these dynamic effects, which often fail to materialise to the extent anticipated. The reduction in the discount rate, which increases the present value of future benefits, illustrates how these views could influence policy. Markets will therefore scrutinise whether the government relies on credible OBR forecasts or uncertain future growth effects to justify additional spending.
Similarly, postponing major commitments, including higher defence expenditure and social care reform, without explaining how they will eventually be financed, could undermine confidence even if the fiscal rules are formally met. 
A negative surprise would likely lead to higher long-dated gilt yields and a weaker pound. The 10- to 30-year segment is particularly sensitive to fiscal risk premia, although reduced issuance at the long end could partly cushion supply pressures. With bond markets already on alert, the reaction could be amplified by broader concerns about government finances. A deterioration in confidence would widen UK government bond spreads against German Bunds and US Treasuries. 
Ultimately, a cautious Budget may help preserve market confidence in the near term but postponing major spending decisions until 2027 risks creating a more difficult fiscal challenge further down the road.

articles.title: Complex risk landscape puts pressure on growth
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
A spinning compass needle in an increasingly complex risk landscape – reflections.
 Global equity markets showed considerable nervousness and 
volatility
 last week. On Friday, the 
S&P 500 closed down 0.5%
 and the 
Nasdaq fell 0.2%
. However, both indices limited their weekly losses to around 0.5%, and 2026 remains a very strong year for equities, with the S&P 500 up 11.4% so far. Overall, companies have delivered 
robust third-quarter earnings
. But the ingredients of the "
risk cocktail
" are familiar: 
(1)
high energy costs
 and 
El Niño
 are increasing 
inflation risks
, 
(2)
 the entire 
yield curve
 has shifted upwards, driven by cyclical, structural and 
political factors
, and 
(3)
 questions remain about 
the sustainability of the AI boom
. The positive economic outlook has not changed significantly, but even an optimist must acknowledge that the scope for disappointment is now greater than usual. Increased financial market volatility is not entirely unwelcome. It reduces the risk of all of us (!) developing tunnel vision and herd mentality. Central banks' shift in monetary policy (more on the Fed below) has helped keep long-term inflation expectations close to their 2% targets. At this stage, a rise in inflation expectations would be particularly troubling for both bond markets and asset prices, adding yet another layer of complexity to the risk landscape. Asian equity markets are trading cautiously early Monday ahead of the Fed and ECB decisions on Wednesday and Thursday. Equity futures are also subdued. 
Asian stock markets are trading cautiously early on Monday ahead of this week’s Fed and ECB policy decisions and a new round of corporate earnings reports. Equity futures are also little changed.
The Fed pauses but keeps its powder dry for December – conclusions.
 On Wednesday, less than a week before the US midterm elections, the Fed is expected to leave its policy rate unchanged at 4.00%, thereby avoiding renewed conflict with the White House. On the one hand, US inflation remains elevated – core PCE stands at 3.0% – although it is not accelerating. On the other hand, financial conditions, which Fed Chair Warsh has shown an interest in as a monetary policy consideration, have tightened due to higher real yields and a modest equity market pullback. Nevertheless, financial conditions remain accommodative. The probability of a "nasty Christmas present" (read: a rate hike) on 9 December now stands at just over 75%. 
Read more about our Fed views here
.
Fresh protests across Europe – better contained in France.
 More than 110,000 people demonstrated in Paris against, among other things, the high cost of living. This time, however, the French authorities were better prepared. Italy, Albania, Greece, Spain and Belgium also saw protests over the weekend.
French debt dynamics are giving economists sleepless nights – conclusions.
 France currently faces an unsustainable long-term public debt trajectory. The 
average maturity
 of its government debt is 8.4 years. The borrowing cost at this maturity is around 4.8%, while France's long-term nominal GDP growth is estimated at 3.0%. Moreover, French productivity growth is extremely anaemic. In other words, a situation where the interest rate (r = 4.8%) exceeds nominal growth (g = 3.0%), alongside persistent budget deficits, is not sustainable in the long run. Interest rates and the budget deficit must come down and/or productivity and growth must pick up (see charts). One small, flickering glimmer of hope: 
Moody's has maintained France's credit rating
 – albeit with warnings.
An interesting ECB meeting, but not because of interest rates – thoughts.
The ECB is expected to leave its policy rate unchanged at 2.50% on Thursday
. But keep an eye on two other, more intriguing questions: 
(1)
 will 
Christine Lagarde
 provide any new signals about a possible early departure as ECB President, and 
(2)
 is the ECB prepared to intervene and purchase French government bonds to support Paris? The ECB should, however, not shield French government bonds from political risk premia.
Stays in office.
 Brazil’s electoral court has declared incumbent 
left-wing President Lula da Silva the winner
 of the presidential run-off against right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, securing 51.8% of the vote against 48.2%. At the time of writing, Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat. The 80-year-old Lula will now serve his fourth term in office.
Nordic key stories
The Swedish Centre Party's coalition talks – conclusions.
Today, 
the 
Party 
is 
due 
to 
report 
to 
the 
Speaker 
of 
the parliament 
on 
the 
progress 
of 
its 
government 
formation 
talks. The 
Centre Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist's preferred coalition already exists in practice in Region Stockholm, where the Centre Party governs alongside the Social Democrats, Greens, Liberals and Christian Democrats. At the national level, however, the situation appears more complicated. Former Prime Minister Carl Bildt noted on Swedish television last week that "it will take a political somersault of monumental proportions to resolve this, or we are heading for a snap election". Although the international situation calls for decisive political action, it is better to resolve the key sticking points before the next government takes office. As for the timetable, the government's budget bill must be submitted by 12 November, with the deadline for alternative budget motions on 27 November. In other words, 
November could be a particularly messy month for fiscal policy in 2027, but we need not worry about negative market reactions
.

articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Snurrande kompassnål i alltmer komplicerat risklandskap – reflektioner.
 Förra veckans globala börser uppvisade påtaglig nervositet och 
volatilitet
. I fredags stängde 
S&P 500 på -0,5%
 och 
Nasdaq på -0,2%
. För veckan som helhet begränsades dock fallet till ca 0,5% (båda indexen) och hittills är 2026 fortfarande ett riktigt bra börsår; t ex S&P 500 +11,4%. Sammantaget har bolagen levererat 
robusta delårsrapporter
 för tredje kvartalet. Men ”
riskcocktailens ingredienser
” är välkända: 
(1)
höga 
energikostnader
 och 
El Niño
 lyfter 
inflationsriskerna
, 
(2)
 hela 
avkastningskurvan
 har tryckts uppåt av konjunkturella, strukturella och 
politiska faktorer
, samt 
(3)
 frågetecken kring 
AI-trendens uthållighet
. De positiva ekonomiska utsikterna har inte förändrats nämnvärt men även en optimist inser att utrymmet för besvikelser nu är större än normalt. Ökad finansiell volatilitet är inte ovälkommen. Den reducerar risken för att vi alla (!) drabbas av tunnelseende och flockbeteenden. Centralbankernas omläggning av räntepolitiken (mer om Fed nedan) har medverkat till att långsiktiga inflationsförväntningar fortfarande ligger nära 2%-målen. Det vore i detta läge bekymmersamt för både räntemarknader och tillgångspriser om även prisförväntningarna stiger. Då tillkommer ytterligare en dimension av komplexitet i risklandskapet. 
Börserna i Asien handlas avvaktande tidig måndag inför bl a veckans Fed- och ECB-besked och nya delårsrapporter. Detsamma gäller börsterminerna.
Fed pausar men har torrt krut för december – slutsatser.
 På onsdag, knappt en vecka före USA:s mellanårsval, väntas
Fed lämna räntan oförändrad på 4,00% och därmed undvika nya konflikter med Vita huset. Å ena sidan: USA-inflationen är förhöjd – kärn-PCE ligger på 3,0% – även om den inte accelererar. Å andra sidan: de finansiella förhållandena, som Fedchefen Warsh visat intresse för som policyparameter, har stramats åt till följd av högre realräntor och viss börsrekyl nedåt. De är dock fortsatt expansiva. Sannolikheten för en ”hård julklapp” (läs räntehöjning) den 9 december är nu drygt 75%. 
Läs mer om våra Fed-tankar 
här
.
Nya protester i Europa – mer kontrollerat i Frankrike.
 I Paris demonstrerade över 110 000 personer mot bl a höga levnadskostnader. Men denna gång var de franska myndigheterna bättre förberedda. Även Italien, Albanien, Grekland, Spanien och Belgien har sett protester under helgen.
Fransk skulddynamik skrämmer ekonomen – slutsatser.
 Frankrike har i dag en långsiktigt ohållbar statsskuldsdynamik. 
Den genomsnittliga löptiden
 på skulden är 8,4 år. Upplåningskostnaden för denna löptid är ca 4,8%. Långsiktig nominell BNP-tillväxt i Frankrike bedöms ligga på 3,0%. Därtill är fransk produktivitetstillväxt extremt syrefattig. Med andra ord: det håller inte i längden att räntan (r = 4,8%) överstiger tillväxten (g = 3,0%) vid fortsatta budgetunderskott. Räntan och budgetunderskottet måste ned och/eller produktiviteten och tillväxten måste upp (se bilder). Ett litet flämtande men positiv ljus i mörkret: 
Moody’s ger Frankrike oförändrat kreditbetyg
 – men med varningar.
Spännande ECB-möte men inte p
g
a räntan – tankar.
ECB väntas lämna styrräntan oförändrad på 2,50% på torsdag
. Men håll ögonen på två andra, mer spännande frågor: 
(1)
 ger 
Christine Lagarde
 nya besked om sin eventuella förtida avgång som ECB-chef, och 
(2)
 är ECB beredd att ingripa och köpa franska statsobligationer för att hjälpa Paris? ECB bör dock inte ”lyfta av” politiska riskpremier från franska räntor.
Sitter kvar.
 Brasiliens valdomstol har utropat den sittande 
vänsterpresidenten Lula da Silva till segrare
 i den andra valomgången över högerkandidaten Flávio Bolsonaro, med siffrorna 51,8% mot 48,2%. Bolsonaro har i skrivande stund vägrat erkänna sig besegrad. Det blir den 80-årige Lulas fjärde mandatperiod.
Sverige
Centerpartiets sondering ska redovisas – slutsatser.
 C-ledaren Elisabeth Thand Ringqvists önskekoalition finns redan i verkligheten, i Region Stockholm, där Centerpartiet styr tillsammans med Socialdemokraterna, Miljöpartiet, Liberalerna och Kristdemokraterna. Läget på riksplanet förefaller mer komplicerat. Förre statsministern Carl Bildt konstaterade i Aktuellt förra veckan att ”det krävs antingen någon saltomortal av pyramidala dimensioner för att lösa ut detta, eller så går vi mot ett extraval”. Även om omvärldsläget kräver politisk handlingskraft är det bättre att försöka reda ut knäckfrågorna innan nästa regering tillträder. Tidsmässigt behöver vi förhålla oss till att budgetpropositionen ska lägga senast den 12 november och budgetmotionerna den 27 november. Det kan m a o bli en 
riktigt rörig november för finanspolitiken 2027, men vi behöver inte oroa oss för negativa marknadsreaktioner

articles.title: October pause followed by December hike
articles.heading: Fed Preview
articles.fulltext:
We expect the Fed to hold policy rates unchanged at the 27-28 October FOMC meeting. After softer comments by some Fed members and recent equity price declines markets are pricing over 90% probability for an unchanged rate. The outlook going forward is more uncertain and will depend on the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, the strength of the US economy and developments in financial conditions. For now, we stick to our view that the Fed will raise rates one more time in December followed by renewed cuts by year-end 2027 and in the first half of 2028. With no change and no new FOMC projections, we may have to wait for more policy clues.
Key points
Policy rate expected on hold at 3.75-4.00%
Markets price more than 90% probability for unchanged
Key policy makers want to pause hikes in October
Declining equity markets and rising real rates could make financial conditions less supportive
Fed usually avoids changing rates directly ahead of elections
Mixed data since September
Members were united behind September decision but not on why
We expect one more hike in December, but the outlook is uncertain
Anything but unchanged rates would be a huge surprise 
At its 15-16 September policy meeting, the Fed raised rates by 25 bps, in the first such move since July 2023. According to the projections (“dot plots”), members expected at least one more rate increase this year, while Chair Kevin Warsh repeated some of his hawkish views from the speech at Jackson Hole in August. This caused markets to price around 50% probability of another rate hike at the next meeting in October. However, calls for a rate pause from key FOMC members – together with a lack of push-back from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh - and jittery equity and debt markets have shifted market expectations ahead of this week’s 27-28 October FOMC policy meeting. Market pricing now indicates over 90% probability that the Fed will leave its Fed funds rate unchanged within the current range of 3.75-4.00%, in line with our long-held forecast.
Risks for dissent from the hawks 
Even if the Fed – or at least its Chair – no longer intends to steer market expectations ahead of meetings, we see it as unlikely that the Fed would want to upset markets with a very unanticipated tightening. Furthermore, we also think that Warsh would prefer the Fed to be unanimous when raising rates to lessen the risks for conflicts with the White House. Recent speeches by the Fed’s vice Chairs John Williams and Philip Jefferson, together with Governor Christopher Waller, suggest they will not support another rate increase already at the October meeting. However, we think at least two members, Beth Hammack and Lorie Logan, may dissent in favour of an increase to take rates one step closer towards a restrictive level.
New communication policy limits scope for policy signals at meetings
With an unchanged policy rate, the focus at the meeting will be on the degree of consensus around the decision and whether there are any changes in the Fed’s policy statement or in the comments from Kevin Warsh at the press conference. We do not expect any clear signals in either the statement or by Kevin Warsh. Still, markets are likely to take notice of whether Warsh repeats his hawkish views from the speech in Jackson Hole and after the September rate decision, or whether he adopts a more neutral language on policy. Otherwise, and given the lack of new projections, we will have to wait for minutes and for comments from individual Fed members. On 16 November, one of Warsh task forces will hold a hearing in San Francisco about productivity and the labour market which may shed further light on new thinking within the Fed. 
Several reasons for an October pause
Our own expectations for unchanged rates have been based on several factors: proximity to the 3 November midterm elections, mixed data and tightening financial conditions after the September meeting and softer signals from Fed members. 
The Fed mostly avoids changing rates directly ahead of elections
The Fed has mostly avoided changing rates directly ahead of federal elections. According to one 
study
, by the derivates marketplace CME Group, the Fed left rates unchanged between 1 October and election day ahead of two thirds of federal elections since 1972. The exceptions to this rule have mainly happened during ongoing tightening cycles and deep crises. Markets have, however, not seen the election as an obstacle given that it temporarily priced a relatively high probability for an October hike. 
Mixed data since September
The Fed’s key inflation measure, the core PCE, was downwardly revised by a larger than expected 0.4%-points in August. Employment growth slowed markedly in August. Because the supply of labour is also slowing, due to an aging domestic population and strict immigration/deportation policies, the Fed is unlikely to start worrying about downside risks to the labour market. But the data implies that the economy may not be as strong as other data have indicated. This could suggest that current policy rates may not be as expansionary as some Fed members have argued. Slower retail sales in September points in the same direction, although one should be careful to draw conclusions from single months. The inflation picture remains worrisome, however. The core PCE still grew at a 3% y/y pace in August, well above target, and the higher-than-expected September CPI, together with increasing price pressures in the PPI, suggests we could see a slight acceleration in the core PCE when September data is published later this week (29 October). The renewed upturn in energy prices has added new upside risks. 
Limited support for October rate increase among key policy makers
Influential Fed members – vice Chairs John Williams and Philip Jefferson and Governor Christopher Waller – have all signaled a possible pause in rate increases in October. The Vice Chair, and president of the New York Fed, John Williams said in his speech on 
29 September
 that there is no urgency after the September rate increase and that the Fed has time to gather more information. Vice Chair Philp Jefferson said in a speech on 
1 October
 that it may take more time for the Fed judge the need for any further adjustments. Governor Christopher Waller on 
October 8
 said the Fed does not need to hike at consecutive meetings. Their policy outlook differed, however, as Jefferson discussed the needs for “any further adjustments”, Williams said he expected “one further upward adjustment … may be appropriate late this year”, while Waller said he anticipated “additional hikes”. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh participated in an 
event
 with the IMF’s managing director Kristalina Georgieva at the IMF meeting in Bangkok, Thailand, on October 16, but did not make any comments on monetary policy. The fact that Warsh refrained from his earlier hawkish comments was seen as dovish by markets. 
Declining equity prices could make financial conditions less supportive
The rapid rise in real yields had started to attract attention among the Fed. However, after the recent week’s declines, yields are back close to the levels around the September decision. Instead, declining equity prices may lead to an unwanted tightening of financial conditions. In the September minutes, Fed members downplayed the rise in long yields. At the same time, many members believed that rising equity prices and tight credit spreads meant that financial conditions remained supportive. The minutes also highlighted the support from equity prices to consumer spending. 
Minutes showed members united behind hike, but differing on why
The decision to raise rates at the September meeting was supported by all FOMC members. Members were less united behind the reasons for their votes to hike, however, or the extent of further rate increases. Many members saw the hike as insurance against the risks that inflation would get stuck above the target. Others saw the rate hike as necessary given their own inflation outlook. Cleveland Fed’s Beth Hammack and the Dallas Fed’s Lorie Logan both seem to be in the latter camp and have argued in recent speeches that the Fed needs to get rates to a restrictive level. 
Hammack
 explicitly argued for “smaller adjustments… relatively quickly”. However, 
Logan
 also said that rising real yields could lessen the need for the Fed to raise rates. But for the other members, the insurance argument point to more cautious and gradual rate increases. 
Most members expected at least two hikes in September
According to the 
September projections
 almost all Fed members (16 out of the 18 that submitted their projections) expected one more rate increase this year, or in total two hikes including the September decision. This sets a high bar for not tightening further. Almost half (8 out of 18) expected two further rate increases, by either year-end 2026 or year-end 2027. Since Fed members project the level of rates by the end of the year, the September median forecast for two hikes could also be consistent with another rate increase in 2027 followed by a cut by year-end 2027.
“Two-and-done”-strategy still our main scenario, but conflict in Middle East is an upside risk 
We stick to our view that the Fed will deliver one more rate increase at the December meeting. In our view, the successive shocks to inflation from tariffs, energy prices and, to some extent, the AI build-out will have only temporary effects on inflation and we continue to expect inflation to return to target, albeit with a delay. Modest wage increases support a return to target for underlying inflation. Inflation expectations remain in line with the target for longer horizons. In such a scenario, we believe the Fed can start easing policy again by end 2027, followed by two more cuts in the first half of 2028 to a neutral level of around 3.25-3.50%. 
Upside risks from the conflict in the Middle East, downside from equities 
The outlook for rates is uncertain, however, with both upside and downside risks. The longer energy prices remain high, the larger the risks that energy costs will spread to other prices through, for instance, higher costs for transportation. Last year, the pass-through of tariffs was smaller than expected, as companies partly absorbed some of the increased import costs in their margins. If high energy prices coincide with strong demand, from both the AI build-out and continued surprisingly resilient households, the ability of companies to pass costs forward to their customers may increase. We have raised our core inflation forecast for both 2026 and 2027, but only slightly. Concerns for a renewed escalation in the conflict in the Middle East have pushed oil prices higher lately. Persistently elevated energy prices, with no end in sight to the conflict in the Middle East, could tip the balance within the Fed for a third increase in rates in early 2027. Continued market unrest, with falling equity and debt markets, and rising household mortgage rates could, on the other hand, prolong the current pause.
Markets have scaled back expectations for rate hikes
At the most, in late September, markets fully priced another 100 bps of hikes until end 2027; now markets are pricing a little above 2 ½ rate increases, with the next step expected to come in December. We see this as more reasonable though still somewhat aggressive compared to our forecast of one more hike in December this year and the medium estimate in the latest FOMC members’ projections in September.
